summary: MIT researchers led by Carlos Díaz-Marín made a polyacrylamide hydrogel loaded with far more lithium chloride than earlier gels, letting it absorb record amounts of water vapor even in dry air. The gel is meant for a passive, electricity-free device that pulls drinking water from air, and the team still has to test how to extract the water. The article also covers worsening water scarcity and other hydrogel uses such as the SmartFarm greenhouse and soil-mixed hydrogels.
one_line: MIT scientists made a super-salty hydrogel that absorbs record moisture from air, aiming for a no-electricity drinking-water device for dry regions.
key_facts: More than one in every four people live in places without enough clean water, and climate change is making this worse.
Carlos Díaz-Marín, a mechanical engineer at MIT in Cambridge, leads a team developing a device to pull water from air affordably without electricity.
The researchers made hydrogel tubes from polyacrylamide, cut them into thin disks, and soaked them in water containing different amounts of lithium chloride.
Earlier tests soaked gels for about two days; Díaz-Marín's team soaked them for up to two months, which made a big difference.
The top-absorbing gel held about three times more salt than previous hydrogels, caching 20 grams (0.7 ounce) of salt per gram of gel.
In relatively dry air like that in deserts, the best-performing hydrogel absorbed 15 percent more water than previous hydrogels.
The findings were reported May 18 in Advanced Materials.
The team still needs to test how to get all the water out of the gels afterward.
By 2050, more than five billion people are expected to lack water at least one month per year.
Swee Ching Tan's team at the National University of Singapore developed SmartFarm, a tiny greenhouse with a moving roof that grows crops without added water; it was used to grow Ipomoea aquatica.
In one study, adding hydrogels to soil reduced by 30 percent how much water was needed to grow food.
The MIT device would capture vapor at night, release it when heated by the sun, condense it on a passively cooled surface, and collect it in a storage chamber.
The team aims for a device that extracts 2 to 5 liters (0.5 to 1.3 gallons) a day, enough for an average person's drinking needs.
